strengths: Novel hierarchical MAB formulation for kernel optimization that naturally decomposes the problem into kernel selection and strategy selection
Principled algorithmic framework seamlessly integrating profiling-guided strategy selection, runtime behavior clustering, and hierarchical UCB with O(K√T ln T) regret bound
Comprehensive experiments across multiple configurations (2 hardware platforms, 2 LLM backends) showing consistent and substantial improvements (2-9× speedup)
Sustained scalability demonstrated through extended optimization trajectories (20 iterations) where KERNELBAND continues improving while baselines saturate
Well-motivated design addressing distinctive challenges (non-stationary rewards, contextual effectiveness, large action space, expensive evaluations)
Rigorous evaluation methodology using TritonBench's framework with multi-shape testing, correctness verification, and statistical robustness
Clear presentation of problem formulation, algorithm design, and intuitive clustering visualization demonstrating meaningful performance similarity within clusters
weaknesses: Critical limitation: only compared against GEAK baseline; no experiments with STARK, EvoEngineer, ConCuR, Kevin, or TritonRL mentioned in related work, making it impossible to assess whether improvements stem from hierarchical MAB formulation or other algorithmic factors

Theoretical analysis relies on formally unstated Assumption 4.1 (cluster-similarity); the bounds depend on terms ϵ_cluster and ϵ_profile that are never empirically measured or validated, undermining tightness claims

Key design choices lack principled justification: K=3 clusters chosen via empirical observation without ablation; α=0.5 parameter weight set arbitrarily without sensitivity analysis; clustering update frequency (Δ=10) unexplained

Reproducibility severely compromised: no code release, depends on LLM API calls (DeepSeek-V3.2, GPT-5.1) that may change, strategy set S never explicitly enumerated, 1000 synthetic warm-up pairs generation process unclear

Severely limited experimental scope: single benchmark (TritonBench with 29 kernels); GPU-only evaluation despite motivation mentioning TPUs and specialized accelerators; only 10-20 iteration budget tested; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals

Missing critical ablations: no ablation on α weighting, number of clusters K, profiling feature sets, or UCB term contributions; insufficient justification for feature engineering choices (why these 9 dimensions for ϕ and 6 for ρ)
Reward function r∈(-∞,1] exhibits problematic asymmetry (unbounded downside) contradicting standard UCB analysis assumptions of bounded [0,1] rewards; impact on convergence analysis unexplored
Method appears specialized to Triton kernels; generalization to CUDA, HIP, or other frameworks unexplored despite claiming broader applicability
Limited analysis depth: case study covers only one kernel (seeded_dropout); no investigation of failure modes or scenarios where KERNELBAND underperforms compared to GEAK
Weak validation of core assumptions: cluster-similarity assumption is strong but never empirically validated; assumption that profiling features predict strategy success never tested

strengths: Novel formulation: First work to cast kernel optimization as hierarchical MAB, providing principled exploration-exploitation framework applicable beyond this domain
Well-integrated multi-component design combining profiling guidance, runtime clustering, and hierarchical UCB with clear synergies between components
Strong theoretical contribution with regret bound O(K|S|√T log T) scaling with clusters rather than pool size, reducing constants exponentially when pool is large

Comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation across two distinct GPU platforms (consumer/datacenter), two LLM backends (open-source/commercial), and 29 diverse kernels with multi-shape testing and statistical robustness
Consistent improvements across all tested configurations (Tables 1-2) demonstrating robustness to hardware and model variations
Superior scalability without saturation: extended experiments show KERNELBAND continues improving through 20 iterations while GEAK plateaus around iteration 10
Rigorous evaluation methodology following TritonBench framework with correctness verification, multi-shape evaluation, and weighted aggregation of results
Clear presentation with well-motivated problem formulation, detailed algorithm description, and careful attention to implementation details
weaknesses: Limited baseline comparison: Only GEAK is compared despite mentioning recent alternatives (ConCuR, Kevin, CUDA-L1, TritonRL); no component baselines to validate MAB formulation itself or isolate improvements from specific mechanisms

Insufficient quantitative ablation studies: Section 5.3 provides visualization and case study but lacks empirical breakdown of individual component contributions (profiling term ψ, clustering, exploration term); no sensitivity analysis for hyperparameters α, buffer B, learning rate η
Unjustified hyperparameter choices: K=3 justified only by post-hoc observation without principled reasoning; α=0.5 fixed without ablation; other parameters (B=500, η=0.1, λ=10⁻⁴) lack justification

Empirical validation gap for theoretical assumptions: Cluster-similarity Assumption 4.1 is stated but never quantitatively validated; tightness of ϵ_cluster bound not characterized; profiling model error ϵ_profile not empirically quantified despite appearing in regret bound
Feature engineering not justified: Nine profiling features and six runtime features are hand-crafted without ablation studies or sensitivity analysis; no discussion of alternative feature sets

Limited scalability analysis: Experiments restricted to 29 kernels with 10-20 iterations; regret bound scales as √T log T suggesting diminishing returns at large T; no analysis of scaling to thousands of kernels or hundreds of iterations

Modest improvements in certain scenarios: Table 1 current-iteration results show small differences in some cases; improvements often more pronounced in best-of-iteration metrics, suggesting advantage from exploration trajectory rather than consistent decision quality
No statistical significance testing: Results lack confidence intervals, error bars, or p-values; improvements could be within noise in some cases
Incomplete failure analysis: No discussion of when KERNELBAND underperforms; compilation failure frequency not reported; impact of asymmetric reward space (-∞ to 1) not discussed
Reproducibility concerns: No code provided; LLM prompts not specified; initialization procedure (1,000 synthetic pairs) lacks detail; difficult to reproduce without supplementary materials
Limited scope: Evaluation restricted to GPU kernels via Triton; generalization to other accelerators or languages unclear; single benchmark (TritonBench) tested

Theory-practice gap: Regret analysis assumes bounded model error but online learning from limited initialization may violate this; cluster-similarity violations and their empirical impact not characterized

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation identifying a fundamental mismatch between LLM code generation and kernel optimization as an exploration-exploitation problem
Solid empirical results: 1.91× speedup on A100, 60.1% Fast@1 success rate, and consistent improvements across 3 GPU architectures and 4 LLM backends (39-140% relative improvement over GEAK)
Rigorous ablation studies convincingly demonstrate the bandit policy is essential (regression to 0.97× without it), validating the core contribution
Evidence of hardware-aware adaptation with platform-specific strategy selection patterns (Table 10, Appendix I), supporting the hardware-informed design
Comprehensive evaluation on 183 kernels with well-designed metrics, careful correctness verification protocols, and cost efficiency analysis
Theoretical contribution providing a regret bound dependent on compact covering number K|S_valid| rather than unbounded kernel space, with rigorous decomposition proof
Extensive reproducibility documentation including hyperparameter choices, implementation details, evaluation protocols, and benchmark construction methodology
weaknesses: Critical assumptions lack empirical validation: Assumption 2 (Lipschitz continuity) is never verified empirically—no measurement of the Lipschitz constant L or evidence that strategy effectiveness varies smoothly with kernel behavior; Assumption 1's bounding function B(k,s) is heuristic without theoretical justification

Theorem 1's regret bound contains uncharacterized constants (Lipschitz constant L, cluster diameter diam(C_i)) that are never empirically measured, and the final bound has an unreduced linear term that may be loose, limiting practical guarantees

Limited baseline comparisons: only GEAK and weak Best-of-N compared; concurrent methods (STARK, TritonForge, CudaForge) unavailable, making it difficult to isolate whether improvements come from the MAB formulation specifically

Clustering design lacks principled justification: K-Means with K=3 chosen 'empirically' without principled selection method; periodic re-clustering every τ=10 iterations has no convergence analysis; no guarantee the clustering satisfies the covering assumption required by theory
Behavioral feature selection φ(k) appears ad-hoc: the 5-dimensional vector is reasonable but not justified; no ablation on feature selection or comparison with alternative representations

Hardware signature design not justified: why specifically SM, DRAM, and L2 throughput? What about other bottlenecks (branch divergence, cache efficiency)? The binary mask threshold θ_sat=75% appears arbitrary without sensitivity analysis

Evaluation scope limitations: benchmark modified (sin_computation removed); PyTorch comparison uses only 30/50 kernels; detailed analysis on 27% subset; no analysis of failure modes or cases where KERNELBAND underperforms

Reproducibility concerns: no code release mentioned; dependency on specific LLM APIs (DeepSeek-V3.2) that may change; uses 'corrected' TritonBench-G differing from original; profiling via NVIDIA Nsight Compute may not reproduce across environments

Limited novelty in components: contextual bandits, K-Means clustering, UCB algorithm, and hardware profiling are all standard techniques; novelty comes primarily from the combination and application domain
